podcast.title: Facing Racial Abuse as a Punk Singer
podcast.body: As a Black female punk singer in the early 1980s, Tina Bell faced significant challenges and endured a lot of racial abuse. Her toughness was a necessity in navigating this hostile environment within the music scene. "She had to be because a Black female punk singer? A lot of racial abuse was hurled at her."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Firsts By Black Artists

podcast.title: Godmother of Grunge and First Female Grunge Frontperson
podcast.body: Tina Bell, a Black woman, fronted the group Bam Bam, which formed in 1983, placing her at the very earliest stages of Grunge in the early 1980s. She is recognized as the genre's first ever female front person and is considered a founder of the sound that defined 1990s rock, earning her the title "Godmother of Grunge." "If we look at things in context of the history of Grunge, she was the genre's first ever female front person."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Firsts By Black Artists

podcast.title: Kurt Cobain as a Roadie
podcast.body: Bam Bam attracted fans, and at one point, a young Kurt Cobain worked as a roadie for the band, highlighting their early presence and connection within the nascent Seattle music scene. "But Bam Bam also had their fans, some kid named Kurt Cobain once worked as a roadie for Bam Bam."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Firsts By Black Artists

podcast.title: Pioneering Recording at Reciprocal Recording
podcast.body: Bam Bam made their first record, the "Villains" EP, in 1984 at Reciprocal Recording. This made them the first Grunge band to record at that studio, which later became famous for hosting bands like Nirvana, Alice in Chains, Soundgarden, The Melvins, and Mudhoney. "They used reciprocal recording, making them the first Grunge band to make music there."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Firsts By Black Artists

podcast.title: Struggles with Recognition and Later Life
podcast.body: Despite their early innovation and connections within the Seattle scene, Bam Bam struggled to gain traction and were largely ignored while other local bands achieved success. Tina left in 1990, moved to England and then the Netherlands, but was deported back to the US. She quit music, divorced, battled depression, alcoholism, and cirrhosis, eventually dying in Las Vegas on October 10, 2012, at age 55, with her possessions tragically lost. "But Bam Bam had a hard time gaining any kind of traction."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Comparison to Tina Bell
xref.body: Some writers have drawn comparisons between Tina Bell, the lead singer of Bam Bam, and Tina Turner. This comparison suggests that Bell's powerful stage presence or vocal style might have resonated with elements reminiscent of Turner's iconic performances. "But then there are some writers who have compared Tina to Tina Turner."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Cessation of Activity
xref.body: Tina Bell fronted BamBam until 1990, just one year before the grunge movement exploded into mainstream popularity. "Tina fronted BamBam until 1990, one year before Grunge exploded."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Black History Month 2023

xref.title: Early Grunge Pioneer
xref.body: Fronted by Tina Bell, Bam Bam was a groundbreaking Seattle band that was "doing the grunge thing" in 1983, predating the genre's mainstream explosion by a couple of years. They performed before major grunge acts like Nirvana, Soundgarden, and Alice in Chains gained prominence. "And they were doing the grunge thing in 1983, a couple of years before that sound really began to catch on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Unsung Heroes of Music: Part 2

xref.title: Early Seattle Grunge Pioneers
xref.body: Formed in Seattle in 1983 by Tina Bell and Tommy Martin, BamBam had an "unmistakably grungy sound" even before the genre was recognized, making them early architects of the grunge aesthetic. "BamBam, led by Tina, was unmistakably grungy in their sound. They had a decent local following, but for some reason, few outside Seattle took them seriously."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Peaked Too Soon - Bands That Were Ahead of Their Time

xref.title: Exclusion from Grunge History
xref.body: Despite their pioneering role, Tina Bell and BamBam were never given the credit they deserved and are almost completely expunged from the history of Grunge. Information about them online is often incorrect, with some mentions even omitting Tina entirely. "Tina and BamBam were Grunge before anyone even started using that word, but Tina and the band were never given the credit they deserve. In fact, they're almost completely expunged from the history of Grunge."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Black History Month 2023

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Unsung Heroes of Music: Part 2

xref.title: Lack of Recognition
xref.body: Despite playing important gigs and festivals, recording at the same studio as Nirvana's first records, winning local music awards, having The Melvins open for them, and even featuring Kurt Cobain at one point, Bam Bam and Tina Bell are almost completely omitted from the history of grunge. Existing online mentions are often incorrect or omit Tina entirely. "But they're almost completely expunged from the history of Grunge."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Unsung Heroes of Music: Part 2

xref.title: Matt Cameron's Recognition of Tina Bell
xref.body: Matt Cameron, who was a member of Bam Bam before joining Soundgarden and Pearl Jam, has actively recognized Tina Bell's legacy. He has spoken about her and has been seen wearing Tina Bell t-shirts, indicating ongoing efforts to acknowledge her contributions to grunge. "And if you've been paying attention to Pearl Jam, you might have heard Matt Cameron talk about Tina or even seen him wearing a Tina Bell t-shirt."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Unsung Heroes of Music: Part 2

xref.title: Pioneers of Grunge
xref.body: BamBam, fronted by Tina Bell, was a Seattle-based band performing their "grunge thing" as early as 1983, predating the widespread recognition of the sound by a couple of years. Tina Bell is rightly considered one of the inventors of Grunge, as their sound existed before the term was even commonly used. "Tina was a Black woman who fronted a very grungy sounding band from Seattle called BamBam, and they were doing their Grunge thing in 1983, a couple of years before that sound really began to catch on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Black History Month 2023

xref.title: Posthumous Recognition as Godmother of Grunge
xref.body: It wasn't until the late 2010s that Tina Bell and BamBam began to receive the credit they deserved for creating the grunge aesthetic in Seattle, with Tina Bell now referred to as "the godmother of grunge" or even "the queen of grunge." "It wasn't until the late 2010s that Tina and BamBam started getting the credit they deserved in creating the whole grunge aesthetic in Seattle. If Francois Hardy could be called the grandmother of grunge, it's no stretch at all to call Tina Bell the godmother of grunge. Some even refer to her as the queen of grunge."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Peaked Too Soon - Bands That Were Ahead of Their Time

xref.title: Pre-dating Major Grunge Bands
xref.body: Bam Bam, with Tina Bell, was active and developing their sound before bands like Nirvana, Soundgarden, and Alice in Chains. Their early contributions to the genre were not recognized in the same way as these later groups. "Tina and Bam Bam were doing their thing before Nirvana, before Soundgarden, before Allison Chains."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Unsung Heroes of Music: Part 2

xref.title: Reasons for Lack of Recognition
xref.body: Several factors may have contributed to BamBam's historical oversight, including Tina Bell being a Black woman fronting a punk-rock band in a male-dominated world, their sound being five years too early, issues with bad management, a record deal that went very wrong, or the band stopping at an inopportune moment. "Maybe because this was a Black woman, fronting this kind of punky rock band in a man's world, or it could be that BamBam sound was five years too early. Bad management might be another problem, a record deal then went very wrong, or maybe they just stopped at the wrong time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Black History Month 2023

Existing online mentions are often incorrect or omit Tina entirely. "But they're almost completely expunged from the history of Grunge."

xref.title: Tina Bell's Biography
xref.body: Tina Bell passed away in 2012. Her son, an Academy Award-winning documentary director, authored a biography about her titled "Conversations with the Grunge Queen." "If you want to know more about Tina who died in 2012, by the way, there's a biography written by her son called Conversations with the Grunge Queen."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Black History Month 2023

xref.title: Tina Bell's Departure and Tragic Death
xref.body: Tina Bell left BamBam in 1990 and quit music entirely, falling on hard times by the 2010s, struggling with depression and alcohol. She tragically died of cirrhosis of the liver in an empty Las Vegas apartment in 2012, with her body not found for a couple of weeks. "Tina left BamBam in 1990 and was not replaced. They continued as an instrumental band. Tina quit music entirely. By the 2010, she'd fallen on hard times, often finding it hard to find a decent place to live. She volunteered at a local church, but still struggled with depression, which she sought to treat with alcohol. She ended up dying of cirrhosis of the liver in an empty Las Vegas apartment in 2012."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Tina Bell's Experience with Racial Abuse
xref.body: Tina Bell, a barely five-foot-black woman fronting a heavy rock band, endured a "sickening" amount of racial abuse, highlighting the significant challenges and prejudices she faced as a pioneer in the music scene. "Tina had an especially rough time. She was a barely five-foot-block woman, fronting a heavy rock band, and the amount of racial abuse she endured was sickening."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
